title: "Zero Trust"
description: "A security approach that continuously verifies access instead of trusting users or systems based on network location."
term: "Zero Trust"
letter: "Z"
category: "AI Security"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Zero trust means a system should not automatically trust a user, device, or
service just because it is inside a network. Access is checked for each
request according to identity, context, and policy.

## Technical explanation

Zero-trust architecture applies explicit authentication and authorization,
least privilege, and continuous monitoring to subjects and resources.
Policies may consider identity, device posture, resource sensitivity, and
request context. It is an architectural approach rather than a single product
or a claim that trust can be eliminated entirely.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

AI workflows connect data stores, model endpoints, notebooks, agents, and
deployment systems. Fine-grained access controls can limit the impact of
compromised credentials or unsafe components and help protect sensitive data
and model artifacts.

## How it works

Authenticate each identity, evaluate access policy for a requested resource,
grant only the needed permissions, and log decisions for monitoring. Use
short-lived credentials and segment services so one compromised component
does not imply broad access.

## Practical example

A training job receives short-lived permission to read one approved dataset
and write to its experiment artifact location. It does not receive broad
credentials to unrelated production systems.

## Common misconceptions

- Zero trust does not mean “trust nobody” without evidence; it means verify
  identity and policy explicitly for resource access.
- Network segmentation alone is not a complete zero-trust architecture.
